▣ Slide 4 · Why automated tests, and why now

10.1Why automated tests, and why now

In Class 6 you compared every engine method with your Phase 1 scripts in a validation table: method, engine value, script value, match. That check was correct, but it was manual and it was done once. From today, the code changes every week: new tools, an API (Application Programming Interface) provider, a workflow. Any change can silently break a method that worked yesterday.

A unit test is a short function that calls one unit of your program (for example StatsEngine.median) with a known input and compares the result with the expected value. An automated test suite is the collection of all unit tests, executed by one command in a few seconds. The suite re-checks every number after every change, so a defect is found minutes after it is introduced, not on the day of the Product Defense.

In software testing, a regression is a defect in behaviour that used to work and stopped working after a change. This meaning is different from the statistical regression of Class 7 (fitting a line). The main purpose of a test suite is to detect regressions.

▣ Slide 5 · pytest in five rules

10.1pytest in five rules

pytest is the testing framework named in the course stack (Appendix D). It finds and runs tests automatically when you follow its naming rules (pytest documentationVirusTotal):

  1. Install it inside the virtual environment with python -m pip install pytest, then pin the version in requirements.txt (for example pytest==9.2.0, the version that pip freeze prints on your machine), so that every computer and GitHub Actions install the same version (pip freezeVirusTotal).
  2. Put tests in the folder tests/, in files named test_*.py (for example tests/test_stats_engine.py).
  3. Name every test function test_..., and describe the behaviour in the name: test_median_of_even_count_averages_the_two_middles.
  4. Check results with the plain Python statement assert expression. If the expression is false, the test fails and pytest prints both values.
  5. Run the suite from the repository root with python -m pytest -q. The python -m form adds the current folder to sys.path, so import jarvis works when the package sits at the root of the repository (good integration practicesVirusTotal).

The output has one character per test: . means passed; F means failed (an assert was false, or the test raised an unexpected exception); E means error (the problem happened outside the test body, for example while preparing a fixture). The last line summarises, for example 8 passed in 0.04s. pytest also returns an exit code to the operating system: 0 when every test passed, 1 when at least one failed, 5 when no test was found (exit codesVirusTotal). GitHub Actions reads this number to mark a commit green or red.

▣ Slide 6 · The shape of one test: prepare, call, check

10.1The shape of one test: prepare, call, check

Every good test has three steps, in this order, and checks one behaviour:

StepWhat you writeExample for the median
1. Prepare (arrange)the input data and, if needed, the objectsxs = [4, 9, 1, 7]
2. Call (act)exactly one call to the method under testresult = StatsEngine.median(xs)
3. Check (assert)the comparison with the expected valueassert result == pytest.approx(5.5)

The expected value must come from outside the code under test: a hand computation, your Brick 4 sheet, or an independent library. A test that computes its expected value with the same method it tests proves nothing.

Keep tests short (about 3 to 8 lines) and independent: a test must not rely on another test having run before it, because pytest may run any test alone (python -m pytest -q -k median).

▣ Slides 7–8 · Floats: pytest.approx

10.1Floats and exceptions: pytest.approx and pytest.raises

Floating-point numbers are stored in binary with about 15 to 17 significant decimal digits (the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 754 standard, Class 6). Two correct computations can differ in the last digit: in Class 6, StatsEngine.std_dev returned 6.352072224780001 and statistics.stdev returned 6.3520722247800006 for the same 55 e-mail runs. An exact comparison with == would report a false failure.

pytest.approx compares with a tolerance. By default the allowed difference is the larger of a relative tolerance of 1e-6 (one millionth of the expected value) and an absolute tolerance of 1e-12 (pytest.approxVirusTotal): assert engine_value == pytest.approx(expected). It is the pytest version of math.isclose (math.iscloseVirusTotal).

Your engines also have guards (Class 6): an impossible input raises ValueError with a message. A test can require that exception with pytest.raises used as a context manager (expected exceptionsVirusTotal):

with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="hourly value must be > 0"):
    EconEngine.break_even_hours(20, 0)

The test passes only if the indented call raises ValueError and the message contains the pattern; match performs a regular-expression search, the same tool as the OfflineProvider in Class 7. A legitimate extreme value is different from an error: EconEngine.payback_months(1120, 0) returns math.inf by design, so the test is assert EconEngine.payback_months(1120, 0) == math.inf.

▣ Slides 9–10 · Edge cases

10.1Edge cases and the oracle

An edge case (or boundary case) is an input at the limit of the valid domain of a method. Methods rarely fail on typical data; they fail at the edges. For JARVIS the useful edge cases are:

  • an empty list (mean, median, SD (Standard Deviation) must raise ValueError, not return 0 or crash with ZeroDivisionError);
  • one element (mean and median return that element; the sample SD (Standard Deviation) needs at least two values);
  • an even number of values (the median averages the two middle values) and an odd number;
  • all values equal (SD (Standard Deviation) = 0, so the coefficient of variation is 0, and the IQR fences collapse);
  • a zero hourly value (break-even must raise ValueError) and a zero monthly saving (payback is math.inf, documented).

A test oracle is an independent, trusted source of the expected value. For StatsEngine the standard statistics module is the oracle (statistics moduleVirusTotal): assert StatsEngine.std_dev(xs) == pytest.approx(statistics.stdev(xs)). Your Brick 4 hand computation is a second oracle: for the scheduling times 14, 17, 12, 16, 16 of staff member S5, the sample variance is 4 and the SD (Standard Deviation) is 2.00. The rule from Class 6 still applies: the engine itself never calls statistics; the oracle belongs only in the tests, otherwise the test would compare the code with itself.

▣ Slide 11 · Test first: red, green, refactor — then CI (Continuous Integration)

10.1Test first: the red–green–refactor loop

Test-Driven Development (TDD) writes the test before the code, in a short loop:

  1. Red: write one test for the next behaviour and run it; it fails, which proves that the test can detect the missing behaviour.
  2. Green: write the simplest code that makes the test pass; run the whole suite.
  3. Refactor: improve names and structure while every test stays green.

You do not have to develop all of JARVIS this way, but you must use the loop for every bug: first write a test that reproduces the bug and fails (red), then fix the code (green). This is exactly how a bug-log entry is closed in Sprint 1 (Lesson 10.2).

In the workshop you add ci.yml (Appendix D.3): GitHub Actions installs your pinned requirements and runs python -m pytest -q on every push. This practice is called continuous integration (CI). A red run marks the commit with a failed check, so the team sees a regression before the morning brief uses the broken code.

▣ Slide 12 · Real-life example 10.1 and Code 10.1
Real-life example 10.1 — Locking the owner's numbers before Sprint 1
Task of the exampleConvert the Class 6 validation table into a pytest suite, so that the numbers the owner of Boréal Studio relies on (e-mail mean 35.15 min, the sample SD (Standard Deviation), break-even 0.714 h = 43 min per user per month, payback) are re-checked automatically after every change.How it relates to the lectureIt applies every element of Lesson 10.1: the three-step test, pytest.approx for floats, pytest.raises for the guards, edge cases and one oracle test against the statistics module.

Situation. On a Thursday evening, a team member simplifies StatsEngine.median: the CSV (Comma-Separated Values) is already sorted by date, so sorted(xs) "looks unnecessary" and is removed. The code still runs. The next morning the dashboard reports a median e-mail triage time of 37 minutes instead of 35, and nobody notices, because no number is obviously absurd.

With a suite. The same change, followed by python -m pytest -q, prints F twice and ends with 2 failed, 6 passed: assert 29 == 35 for test_median_of_odd_count and assert 5.0 == 5.5 ± 5.5e-06 for test_median_of_even_count_averages_the_two_middles. The developer restores the sort before committing. If the commit had been pushed, ci.yml would have marked it red on GitHub.

What the team builds. Eight tests: five for StatsEngine (mean of three values, mean of an empty list, median of an odd count, median of an even count, SD (Standard Deviation) against the oracle) and three for EconEngine (break-even of the paid tier, break-even with a zero hourly value, payback with a zero saving). Three of the eight are edge cases and one is an oracle test, which is more than Brick 9 requires.

Code 10.1 — test_engines_demo.py: eight pytest tests for StatsEngine and EconEngine

The player replays a real run of the file, recorded line by line; long loops are shortened. Pause at any moment and click a step to see its line, variables and output.

Step-by-step explanation of Code 10.1

  1. Imports. math, statistics (the oracle), sys and pytest are imported. REPRODUCE_BUG is the only difference between the two scenarios.
  2. The engines. StatsEngine and EconEngine hold static methods. Every method starts with a guard clause that raises ValueError with a message for an impossible input; payback_months returns math.inf for a zero saving because that value is legitimate and documented.
  3. The bug switch. In median, the expression list(xs) if REPRODUCE_BUG else sorted(xs) keeps the original order in scenario A, which is exactly the Class 6 bug, and sorts a copy in scenario B.
  4. Collection. pytest imports the file and collects the eight functions whose names start with test_. The player shows each test as a tile: grey before it runs, amber while it runs, green when it returns normally, red when an exception leaves it.
  5. Normal and edge cases. test_mean_of_three follows prepare → call → check. test_mean_of_empty_list_raises and test_break_even_rejects_zero_hourly_value pass only because pytest.raises sees the expected ValueError with a matching message.
  6. The oracle. In test_std_dev_matches_the_oracle, oracle = statistics.stdev(xs) comes from the independent module; the panel Oracle check shows both values (2.0 and 2.0) and the tolerance band of pytest.approx.
  7. Scenario A. median([35, 29, 41]) returns 29 and median([4, 9, 1, 7]) returns 5.0; the two asserts raise AssertionError, the tiles turn red, and the console ends with 2 failed, 6 passed. pytest's report shows the failing comparison (assert 29 == 35, assert 5.0 == 5.5 ± 5.5e-06).
  8. Scenario B. With the sort restored, every test returns normally and the console prints eight dots and 8 passed. The exit code is 0, the value GitHub Actions turns into a green check.

Figure 10.1

Key terms

unit test — A short function that calls one unit of code with a known input and compares the result with the expected value.
automated test suite — All the tests of a project, executed by one command (python -m pytest -q).
regression (software) — A defect in behaviour that worked before a change; not the statistical regression of Class 7.
assert — Python statement that raises AssertionError when its expression is false; pytest reports it as a failure.
pytest.approx — Comparison with a tolerance: relative 1e-6 or absolute 1e-12 by default.
pytest.raises — Context manager that passes only if the indented code raises the given exception (optionally with a matching message).
edge case — An input at the limit of the valid domain: empty, one element, zero, all values equal.
test oracle — An independent source of the expected value, such as the statistics module or a hand computation.
exit code — Number a program returns to the operating system; pytest returns 0 (all passed), 1 (failures) or 5 (no tests).
continuous integration (CI) — Running the test suite automatically on every push, here with GitHub Actions and ci.yml.

10.2Part 2

When the program stops: tracebacks, the debugger, validation and the bug log

0:15–0:26 lecture · 0:26–0:30 visualization + fun quiz
When JARVIS crashes, how do we find the line that matters, fix the cause instead of the symptom, and prove that the bug stays fixed?
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Read a traceback from the bottom up to the first frame that belongs to your own code.
  • Pause a program with breakpoint() or a VS Code breakpoint and inspect variables one line at a time.
  • Replace a crash on bad input with a validation message, and record the bug in a bug log entry that is closed by a test.
▣ Slide 14 · Exceptions, the call stack and the traceback

10.2Exceptions and the traceback

When an operation cannot be completed, Python creates an exception: an object of a class such as ValueError or KeyError that describes the problem. The program raises the exception at the line where the problem occurred. If no try/except block handles it, the program stops and Python prints a traceback (Errors and ExceptionsVirusTotal).

A program in execution keeps a call stack: one stack frame for each function call that has started and not yet returned (the module, then main(), then load_entries(), then parse_row(), and so on). The traceback lists these frames from the oldest call at the top to the most recent call at the bottom, which is why it begins with Traceback (most recent call last):. Each frame shows the file, the line number, the function and the source line. The last line names the exception type and its message.

▣ Slide 15 · Read it from the bottom: four steps

10.2Read it from the bottom: a four-step procedure

Use the same four steps for every traceback:

  1. Read the last line: the exception type and the message. ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '' means that int() received a text that is not a whole number, here the empty string ''.
  2. Read the frame just above it: file, line and source of the statement that raised the exception.
  3. Move up to the first frame in your own files (jarvis/…, analysis/…, your test files). Frames inside the Python installation or inside site-packages almost never contain the defect; the defect is usually the value your code passed to them.
  4. Ask where the wrong value came from: data file → loader → parser → engine. Follow it backwards until you find the first place where the program should have rejected it.

Since Python 3.11, the traceback also underlines the failing expression with ^ and ~ characters under the source line (PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 657VirusTotal). In int(raw) the marks sit under the call, which confirms that the failing value is raw.

▣ Slide 16 · The exceptions you will meet in JARVIS

10.2The exceptions you will meet in JARVIS

ExceptionTypical cause in JARVISWhere to fix it
ValueErrorint(""), int("17.0"), date.fromisoformat("2026/09/14")validate the field in the loader or parser
KeyErrorrow["minute"] (misspelt column), tools["book_flight"] (unknown intent)check the header; handle unknown intents with a clear reply
TypeErrorNone + 1; a text passed where a number is expectedconvert types at the boundary; type hints show the intent
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute ...a function returned None: cursor.fetchone() found no row, re.match() found no matchtest for None right after the call
FileNotFoundErrora relative path run from another working folderbuild paths with pathlib from the location of the file
ZeroDivisionErrora mean of an empty group without a guardguard: raise ValueError with a message
sqlite3.OperationalError: no such tablethe database file was not initialised, or a wrong path created an empty filecreate the schema at start-up; check the path
json.JSONDecodeErroran API (Application Programming Interface) answer that is not JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) (Lesson 10.3)catch it and fall back to the OfflineProvider

Most of these exceptions are raised at one line but caused several frames earlier, where the wrong value entered the program (built-in exceptionsVirusTotal).

▣ Slides 17–18 · The debugger (1/2): breakpoint() and pdb

10.2The debugger: pause, look, step

A debugger runs your program under control. It stops at a breakpoint, a marked line, before executing it; it shows the value of every variable in every frame; and it executes the program one line at a time. A traceback shows the frames after the program has stopped; a debugger shows the same frames while the program is still running.

With breakpoint() (built in since Python 3.7, PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 553VirusTotal): write breakpoint() on the line before the suspected problem and run the program. Python opens the pdb prompt (pdb documentationVirusTotal). The commands you need:

CommandEffect
n (next)execute the current line, stop at the next line of the same function
s (step)enter the function called on the current line
c (continue)run until the next breakpoint
p rawprint the value of an expression, here the variable raw
l (list)show the source lines around the current line
w (where)print the call stack, most recent frame at the bottom
q (quit)stop the program

With VS Code: click to the left of a line number (a red dot appears), open Run and Debug and choose Python Debugger: Debug Python File (F5). The Variables, Watch and Call Stack panes show the state; the toolbar steps over (F10), into (F11) and out of (Shift+F11) a call (VS Code Python debuggingVirusTotal). Remove every breakpoint() line before committing: a forgotten one stops the scheduled workflow, which has no keyboard.

▣ Slide 19 · Input validation at the boundary

10.2Input validation: reject bad data at the boundary

Input validation checks that data coming from outside the program (a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) row, a command typed by a staff member, an API (Application Programming Interface) answer) has the expected type, range and format before the program uses it. The check belongs at the boundary, the first function that receives the outside data: the loader, the command parser, the provider.

A good validation message names the place, the field, the rule and the value: line 4: minutes must be a whole number >= 0, got ''. A message such as error or invalid input forces the reader to debug again.

Decide what happens after a rejection:

  • One bad row in a batch (the loader): skip the row, count it, report it at the end. One typing error must not stop the morning brief for the whole studio.
  • A bad configuration (no database file, no tests/ folder in CI (Continuous Integration)): stop immediately with a clear message, because every later step would be wrong.

The validation itself is written as a guard clause: test for the bad case first and leave the function (raise or return) before the normal path, so the normal path stays unindented and readable (Class 6).

▣ Slides 20–21 · The bug log

10.2The bug log and the debugging loop

A bug log is a table with one row per defect. The course template (docs/buglog.md) has these columns: ID (identifier) · date · symptom (what the user saw) · cause (the defect in the code or the data) · fix (what changed, with the commit) · test (the test that proves the fix) · status.

The symptom and the root cause are different things. Symptom: "the morning brief stopped at 06:30". Root cause: "the loader converted the minutes with int() without checking for an empty cell". Fixing the symptom (restarting the workflow) leaves the cause in place.

A bug is closed only when a test reproduces it: the test fails before the fix and passes after it. "Fixed, but no test" stays open, because a later change can bring the defect back without anyone noticing (a regression, Lesson 10.1).

The loop you will use in Sprint 1:

  1. Reproduce: run the same command with the same input until the failure appears every time.
  2. Read the traceback with the four-step procedure.
  3. Isolate: reduce the input to the smallest case that still fails; use the debugger to watch the wrong value appear.
  4. Fix the cause at the boundary.
  5. Prove: the new test is red without the fix and green with it.
  6. Log: add the bug-log row and commit the fix, the test and the log together.
▣ Slide 23 · Activity 2 — Fun quiz: anatomy of a traceback
Activity 2 — Anatomy of a traceback, then three quick questions0:26–0:30Visualization + fun quiz

Look at Figure 10.2 (the traceback of the morning brief) for one minute and point to: the last line, the frame that raised the exception, and the first frame in our own file. Then answer the three questions out loud:

  1. Which line of a traceback do you read first?
  2. AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'minutes' — what does it tell you about the variable before .minutes?

▣ Slide 22 · Real-life example 10.2 and Code 10.2
Real-life example 10.2 — The morning brief that stopped at 06:30
Task of the exampleA staff member typed a row in data/new_entries.csv and left the minutes cell empty. The scheduled morning brief crashed. The team must read the traceback, locate the first frame in its own code, add validation that skips and reports the row, prove the fix with a test and record BUG-004 in the bug log.How it relates to the lectureIt applies the four-step traceback procedure, validation at the boundary, the symptom/cause distinction and the rule that a bug is closed only by a test.

Symptom. At 06:30 the workflow log ends with a traceback, and the owner receives no brief. The last line reads ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: ''.

Reading. The frame above the last line is parse_row, at the statement int(raw). Moving up: load_entries called parse_row for the row at line 4 of the file, and main called load_entries. All three frames are in our own file, so the defect is ours: parse_row converts the text without checking it.

Fix at the boundary. parse_row now checks the text with a guard clause and raises ValueError("minutes must be a whole number >= 0, got ''"); load_entries catches that error for one row, skips the row and records line 4: … in a list of skipped rows; the brief prints the four valid rows and one "skipped" line.

Proof and log. The test test_parse_row_rejects_empty_minutes uses pytest.raises. It fails on the old code (the message does not match) and passes on the new code. The bug-log row is: BUG-004 | brief stopped at 06:30 | int('') on an empty minutes cell | guard clause + skip and report | test_parse_row_rejects_empty_minutes | closed.

  • a fixed parse_row/load_entries with a validation message that names line, field, rule and value

Scenario B runs the fixed version: parse_row validates the field with a guard clause, load_entries skips and reports the bad row, the brief continues with four rows, the test that proves the fix passes, and the bug-log row BUG-004 is printed.

Step-by-step explanation of Code 10.2

  1. Data. NEW_ENTRIES holds a header and five rows; the row at line 4 has an empty minutes cell. io.StringIO lets csv.DictReader read the text like a file.
  2. The call stack grows. main() calls load_entries(), which calls parse_row() once per row. The panel Call stack shows one box per active call: this pile is exactly what a traceback prints.
  3. Scenario A — the exception. For the row of S3, raw is '' and int(raw) raises ValueError. The exception leaves parse_row, then load_entries, then main (each frame turns red), and reaches the module level, where Python prints the traceback.
  4. Reading the traceback. Bottom line: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: ''. Frame above: line 40 in parse_row. All frames are in our file, so the defect is ours: parse_row converts the text without checking it.
  5. Scenario B — validation. parse_row strips the text and applies the guard clause if not raw.isdigit(): raise ValueError(...). The message names the field, the rule and the value.
  6. Skip and report. In load_entries, try/except ValueError surrounds one row only: the row at line 4 is appended to skipped with its line number, and the loop continues. The panel Rows shows four green rows and one red row.
  7. The brief continues. morning brief: 4 runs, 79 min logged (34 + 9 + 21 + 15), followed by skipped line 4: minutes must be a whole number >= 0, got ''.
  8. Proof and log. test_parse_row_rejects_empty_minutes uses pytest.raises(..., match="whole number"); it would fail on version A (different message) and passes on version B. The last line is the bug-log row with status closed.

Figure 10.2

Key terms

exception — An object (for example ValueError) that Python raises when an operation cannot be completed.
traceback — The printed list of stack frames from the oldest call (top) to the most recent (bottom), ending with the exception type and message.
stack frame — The record of one active function call: file, line, function and local variables.
debugger — A tool that runs the program under control: breakpoints, variable inspection, step-by-step execution.
breakpoint — A marked line where the debugger pauses before executing it.
pdb — The Python debugger in the standard library, opened by breakpoint().
input validation — Checking type, range and format of outside data before the program uses it.
guard clause — A check at the start of a function that leaves early (raise or return) on bad input.
bug log — A table of defects: ID (identifier), date, symptom, cause, fix, test, status.
root cause — The defect that produces the symptom; fixing it removes the symptom permanently.

10.3Part 3

JARVIS goes online: the ApiProvider, the key and the scheduled workflow

0:30–0:41 lecture · 0:41–0:45 zen break + flash cards
How can JARVIS use a free language-model service and run every weekday at 06:30 on GitHub, without ever depending on that service or exposing the key?
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain how ApiProvider produces the same Intent as OfflineProvider through one HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) POST request, and why every failure falls back to OfflineProvider.
  • Keep the API (Application Programming Interface) key out of the code: an environment variable on your computer, a repository secret on GitHub.
  • Read jarvis.yml line by line: schedule (cron in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time)), workflow_dispatch, permissions, the commit of data/jarvis.db and [skip ci].
▣ Slide 24 · One contract, two implementations

10.3One contract, two implementations

In Classes 5 and 7 you defined the abstract base class Provider with one method, parse(text) -> Intent, and implemented OfflineProvider with regular expressions and a keyword table. It is deterministic: the same text always gives the same Intent, which makes it testable.

ApiProvider is a second subclass with the same method. Instead of rules, it sends the request text to a large language model (LLM), a statistical model of text that is offered as a web service, and asks it to answer with the intent and its arguments as JSON (JavaScript Object Notation). The Agent does not change at all: it calls provider.parse(text) and receives an Intent, whichever subclass it holds. This is polymorphism, and a Provider hierarchy with two working subclasses is one of the elements the rubric lists for the "Exemplary" level of Tech Implementation.

▣ Slides 25–26 · One HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) request (1/2): the four parts

10.3One HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) request, part by part

The ApiProvider talks to the service through an API (Application Programming Interface) (Application Programming Interface): a set of addresses and rules that one program offers to other programs. The messages travel with HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) (Hypertext Transfer Protocol). One request has four parts (IBM (International Business Machines) Technology videoVirusTotal):

PartIn the ApiProvider
methodPOST: send data to be processed
URL (Uniform Resource Locator) (address)the provider's base URL followed by /chat/completions
headersAuthorization: Bearer <key> and Content-Type: application/json
bodya JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) object: the model name, temperature 0 and two messages, the system instructions and the staff member's text

The answer has a status code and a body. The codes you must recognise: 200 success; 401 the key was refused; 429 Too Many Requests, the provider's rate limit was exceeded, often with a Retry-After header that gives the seconds to wait (MDN: 429VirusTotal); 5xx an error on the provider's server.

"OpenAI-compatible" means that the provider accepts the request format of OpenAI's Chat Completions endpoint, so one ApiProvider class works with several providers by changing the base URL (Uniform Resource Locator) and the model name. Groq documents the base URL https://api.groq.com/openai/v1 (GroqVirusTotal) and the Gemini API (Application Programming Interface) documents https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai/ (Gemini APIVirusTotal). In the answer, the text of the model is at data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]; the ApiProvider decodes it with json.loads, checks that the intent is a known tool name, and builds the Intent.

Temperature controls how much the model varies its wording: 0 makes it choose the most probable output, which reduces variation between runs but does not make the model deterministic. That is one more reason why the tests and the Mid-Term use the OfflineProvider.

With the standard library only, the request is two calls: urllib.request.Request(url, data=json.dumps(body).encode(), headers=..., method="POST") and urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=10) (urllib.requestVirusTotal). An answer with status 400 or higher raises urllib.error.HTTPError; no network raises urllib.error.URLError; no answer in time raises TimeoutError.

▣ Slides 27–28 · The fallback rule

10.3The fallback rule and the free tier

The ApiProvider follows one rule: any failure returns the OfflineProvider's answer. The failures are: no key (no request is sent at all), HTTPError (401, 429, 5xx), URLError (no network), TimeoutError, json.JSONDecodeError (the model answered text that is not JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)), and KeyError or ValueError (JSON without the expected fields, or an intent that is not a tool). Every run is written to the runs table with provider = "api" or provider = "offline" (Appendix D.2), so the team can count how often the fallback was used.

A fallback is a planned, tested path, not an error. It implements the non-functional requirement of Brick 2: JARVIS works with no key and no network. This is also why the Final defense may be run offline.

Free tiers are limited per period: requests per minute (RPM), requests per day (RPD) and tokens per minute (TPM); a token is a piece of a word, the unit in which models count text. Exceeding any limit returns HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) 429 (Groq rate limitsVirusTotal, Gemini API (Application Programming Interface) rate limitsVirusTotal). Limits differ between providers and change over time, so read the provider's rate-limit page the week you connect, and record the numbers with the date in docs/econ_notes.md: they are inputs to your break-even model (Class 3), not constants.

Watch outThe course schedule names three free providers. One of them, GitHub Models, is no longer available: GitHub's documentation states that it was fully retired on July 30, 2026 (GitHub Models noticeVirusTotal). Use Groq or the Gemini API (Application Programming Interface).
▣ Slide 29 · The key never enters the repository

10.3The key never enters the repository

An API (Application Programming Interface) key is a secret text that identifies your account to the provider; anyone who has it can spend your quota. It must never appear in the code, in a committed file, in a screenshot or in the report.

An environment variable is a named value that the operating system gives to a program when the program starts. The ApiProvider reads os.environ.get("JARVIS_API_KEY"), which returns None when the variable is not set (os.environVirusTotal). On your computer you set the variable in the terminal session, or in a .env file that is listed in .gitignore. Keeping configuration in the environment, outside the code, is a widely used rule of software engineering (The Twelve-Factor AppVirusTotal).

On GitHub, the same name is stored as a repository secret: Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret (GitHub secretsVirusTotal). The workflow passes it to one step with env: JARVIS_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.JARVIS_API_KEY }}. Secrets are not passed to workflows that run for pull requests from forks, which protects the key from strangers.

If a key was ever committed, it stays in the Git history even after you delete the file. Create a new key and delete the old one the same day (this is called rotating the key). Use only your own account and keys, and respect the provider's terms of use (Legal Notice §6).

▣ Slides 31–33 · jarvis.yml (1/3): when it runs

10.3jarvis.yml, line by line

A workflow is a YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) file in .github/workflows/ that tells GitHub Actions when to run a job and which steps to execute on a fresh virtual machine called a runner. The JARVIS workflow (Appendix D.3) has four parts:

When. schedule: - cron: '30 11 * * 1-5'. A cron expression has five fields: minute, hour, day of the month, month, day of the week. This one means minute 30 of hour 11, every day of the month, every month, Monday to Friday (1-5). GitHub evaluates schedules in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) (Coordinated Universal Time) by default, so the run starts at 06:30 in Montréal in winter (EST (Eastern Standard Time), UTC−5) and at 07:30 in summer (EDT (Eastern Daylight Time), UTC−4). Scheduled runs may start late when GitHub is busy, especially at the start of an hour, which is one reason to choose minute 30; the shortest interval is 5 minutes, and schedules run on the latest commit of the default branch (schedule eventVirusTotal). workflow_dispatch: adds a Run workflow button, which you use to test the workflow without waiting for the schedule.

With which rights. permissions: contents: write allows the job's built-in token, GITHUB_TOKEN, to push a commit. Without this line the final git push is rejected.

What. checkout → setup-python 3.12 → pip install -r requirements.txt → python -m jarvis brief (the step that receives the secret) → python -m jarvis report (regenerates docs/dashboard.html and the charts).

Commit-back. The job sets the author to github-actions[bot], stages data/ and docs/, then runs git diff --cached --quiet || git commit -m 'jarvis: morning brief [skip ci]' and git push. git diff --cached --quiet exits with 0 when nothing is staged, and || runs the commit only when the previous command failed, so a day without changes does not produce an empty-commit error.

No loop. The commit message contains [skip ci], which tells GitHub to skip workflows triggered by push and pull_request for that commit, so ci.yml does not run (skipping workflow runsVirusTotal). In addition, events caused by the GITHUB_TOKEN do not create new workflow runs, except workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch (GitHub documentationVirusTotal). These are two independent protections.

Keep it alive. In a public repository, GitHub disables scheduled workflows after 60 days without activity (disabling workflowsVirusTotal); the bot's daily commit counts as activity. The tiny-database rule still applies: one writer at a time, git pull before you run JARVIS locally; if a push is rejected, git pull --rebase and run the command again, never merge two .db files by hand.

▣ Slide 34 · The dashboard on GitHub Pages

10.3The dashboard on GitHub Pages

python -m jarvis report writes docs/dashboard.html, a self-contained page with the charts embedded. GitHub Pages can publish the docs/ folder as a website: Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → branch main, folder /docs (GitHub PagesVirusTotal). On GitHub Free, Pages works only for public repositories; private repositories need GitHub Pro or a team plan (GitHub Pro is part of the free GitHub Student Developer Pack). The alternative is to keep the team repository private and copy only docs/dashboard.html to a separate public repository.

The dashboard shows aggregated numbers only: averages per routine, totals per day. No staff member's individual rows, no personal time log and no message text are ever published (Legal Notice §20 Personal information).

▣ Slide 35 · Real-life example 10.3 and Code 10.3
Real-life example 10.3 — The 06:30 brief that runs without anyone
Task of the exampleThe owner wants the morning brief at 06:30 every weekday, and she wants it even on days when the free API (Application Programming Interface) tier refuses requests. The team implements ApiProvider with an injected transport, tests three paths (answer 200, rate limit 429, no key), logs the provider used for each run, and schedules jarvis.yml.How it relates to the lectureIt applies the anatomy of an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) request, the fallback rule, the environment variable and repository secret, and the cron schedule of jarvis.yml.

Monday. The workflow starts at 11:30 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time). The key is present, the provider answers 200 with {"intent": "log_time", "args": {"minutes": 25, "routine": "email_triage"}}, and the runs table receives a row with provider = api.

Tuesday. The team has run many experiments: the provider answers 429 Too Many Requests. ApiProvider catches the HTTPError, calls OfflineProvider, and the regular expression of Class 7 extracts the same Intent. The brief arrives; the row says provider = offline.

Wednesday. While rotating the key, a member deletes the secret before creating the new one. os.environ.get("JARVIS_API_KEY") returns None, no request is sent, OfflineProvider answers, and the brief still arrives.

Why this design is testable. The ApiProvider receives its transport (the function that sends the HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) request) as a constructor argument, a technique called dependency injection (Class 5). The tests pass a fake transport that returns a prepared answer or raises a prepared error, so the three days above become three fast, repeatable tests that never use the network and never need a key.

Deliverables you will produce

  • jarvis/providers.py with ApiProvider(base_url, model, api_key, transport) and the fallback rule
  • tests/test_providers.py with three fake-transport tests (200, 429, no key) and two OfflineProvider.parse tests
  • the repository secret JARVIS_API_KEY (screenshot of the settings page, value hidden)
  • .github/workflows/jarvis.yml with the schedule, workflow_dispatch and contents: write; one successful run with the bot's commit

Scenario rate_limited: it raises HTTPError 429 and the OfflineProvider answers (provider = offline). Scenario no_key: no request is sent and the OfflineProvider answers. The real urllib_transport function is included for Sprint 1.

Visualization · Request flow and the runs table

The player replays a real run of the file, recorded line by line; long loops are shortened. Pause at any moment and click a step to see its line, variables and output.

Step-by-step explanation of Code 10.3

  1. Configuration from the environment. BASE_URL, MODEL and API_KEY are read with os.environ.get, the same names as the repository secret and variables of jarvis.yml. The default key is a fake text; in scenario no_key the key is set to None.
  2. Two providers, one method. OfflineProvider.parse uses the Class 7 regular expression. ApiProvider.parse has the same signature and returns the same Intent, so the Agent works with either (polymorphism).
  3. Injection. ApiProvider receives transport in its constructor. main passes FakeTransport(SCENARIO); Sprint 1 passes urllib_transport, which sends a real POST with urllib.request.
  4. Day 1 (ok). The body (model, temperature 0, system and user messages) goes to .../chat/completions. The fake answer has the Chat Completions structure; json.loads decodes the model's text, the intent log_time is checked against TOOLS, and last_provider becomes api.
  5. Day 2 (rate_limited). The transport raises HTTPError 429. The except clause catches it, prints api failed (HTTPError: HTTP Error 429: Too Many Requests) -> offline fallback and calls the OfflineProvider, which extracts the same intent from the text.
  6. Day 3 (no_key). The guard clause if not self.api_key returns the OfflineProvider's answer before any request is built; the log says no request sent.
  7. The Agent loop. Agent.handle runs provider.parse → looks up the tool → LogTimeTool.run → appends a runs row. The panel Flow lights the path taken; the runs table shows provider = api or offline.
  8. What to observe. The reply is identical on the three days (logged 25 min of email_triage); only the provider column differs. This is the non-functional requirement "works with no key and no network" made visible.
▣ Slide 30 · How the 06:30 brief travels — and where the key lives

Figure 10.3

Key terms

ApiProvider — Provider subclass that obtains the Intent from a language-model API (Application Programming Interface); falls back to OfflineProvider on any failure.
HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) status code — Number in the answer: 200 success, 401 key refused, 429 rate limit exceeded, 5xx server error.
OpenAI-compatible endpoint — A provider address that accepts the Chat Completions request format (Groq, Gemini API (Application Programming Interface)).
fallback — The planned path taken when the preferred path fails; here OfflineProvider, logged as provider = offline.
environment variable — A named value the operating system gives to a program at start; read with os.environ.get().
repository secret — An encrypted value stored in the repository settings and passed to workflow steps with ${{ secrets.NAME }}.
cron expression — Five fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week); '30 11 * * 1-5' = 11:30 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) on weekdays.
permissions: contents: write — Workflow setting that lets GITHUB_TOKEN push commits, required for the commit-back of jarvis.db.
[skip ci] — Text in a commit message that makes GitHub skip push and pull_request workflows for that commit.
rate limit — The maximum number of requests or tokens allowed per period; exceeding it returns HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) 429.

click or press Enter to flip

Lesson 10.3 · card 2 / 5
Name the four parts of the HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) request that ApiProvider sends.
click or press Enter to flip
Answer
Method POST; URL (Uniform Resource Locator) = base URL + /chat/completions; headers Authorization: Bearer <key> and Content-Type: application/json; body = JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) with the model, temperature 0 and the messages.
Lesson 10.3 · card 3 / 5
What does status 429 mean, and what does JARVIS do?
click or press Enter to flip
Answer
Too Many Requests: the rate limit of the free tier was exceeded (often with Retry-After). ApiProvider catches the HTTPError and returns the OfflineProvider's answer, logged as provider = offline.
Lesson 10.3 · card 4 / 5
Where does the API (Application Programming Interface) key live on your computer and on GitHub?
click or press Enter to flip
Answer
In the environment variable JARVIS_API_KEY (terminal session or a git-ignored .env file) and in the repository secret JARVIS_API_KEY; never in code or in a committed file.
Lesson 10.3 · card 5 / 5
Why does the bot's commit not start ci.yml again?
click or press Enter to flip
Answer
The message contains [skip ci], so GitHub skips push and pull_request workflows for it; and events caused by GITHUB_TOKEN do not create new workflow runs anyway.

10.4Part 4

From results to a decision: charts, the recommendation, the technical report and the three sprints

0:45–0:56 lecture · 0:56–1:00 short practical
How do the numbers of JARVIS become an answer to each research question, a decision the owner can act on, and a technical report that the Final will grade?
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Choose the chart that answers each research question and give it a numbered caption.
  • Write a recommendation with its expected impact in hours and dollars per month, its risks and the alternatives considered.
  • Map every Brick to a section of the technical report and state the goals and deadlines of the three Project Sprints.
▣ Slide 37 · Results, discussion, conclusions

10.4Results, discussion and conclusions are three different things

Your project has three research questions (RQ (Research Question)), refined in Brick 2. RQ1 (Research Question 1) asks which routines cost the most time and which vary the most (statistics). RQ2 (Research Question 2) asks what an hour of staff time is worth, what automation costs and where the break-even between the free tier and a paid assistant lies (microeconomics). RQ3 (Research Question 3) asks which routines JARVIS should automate first, how much time it saves and what the risk is (integration).

A result is a number or a table together with its evidence (the data, the method, the sample size n) and its limits. A discussion interprets the results for the reader: what they mean for the owner, whether they match what was expected, and what could make them wrong. A conclusion answers one research question in one or two sentences, using only results already presented: no new data and no new analysis appear in a conclusion.

▣ Slide 38 · Which chart answers which question

10.4Which chart answers which question

A chart is chosen by the question it must answer, not by its appearance (Figure 10.4):

Question typeChartJARVIS example
compare categoriesbar chart, bars sorted, axis starting at zeromonthly cost per routine (RQ1 (Research Question 1))
change over timeline chart, time on the horizontal axismean e-mail minutes per day, pilot and comparison group
relationship between two numeric variablesscatter plot with the fitted line (Class 7)interruptions and minutes of the stand-up notes
effect of a changebefore/after bars for the changed group and the comparison groupe-mail triage before and after the pilot (RQ3 (Research Question 3))

Four rules apply to every chart: one message per chart; axis titles with units (minutes, $ per month); a numbered caption (Figure 3. followed by a short title in italics, as APA (American Psychological Association) recommends — APA figure setupVirusTotal); and a sentence in the text that cites it ("As Figure 3 shows, …"). A chart that the text never mentions is removed. On the public dashboard every chart uses aggregated numbers only.

▣ Slides 39–40 · The numbers behind the decision

10.4The numbers behind the decision

With the teaching copy of the dataset (boreal_routines_2026.csv, 420 runs) the three answers are:

RQ (Research Question)ResultEvidence
RQ1 (Research Question 1)e-mail triage is the most expensive routine: 1 640.12 $ per month, 28.2 % of the routine bill of 5 821.45 $mean minutes per routine × 100 runs per month × 28 $/h ÷ 60 (manual and template runs)
RQ1 (Research Question 1)the stand-up notes vary the most: coefficient of variation (CV) 26.4 %sample SD (Standard Deviation) ÷ mean of the manual runs
RQ2 (Research Question 2)one hour of staff time is worth 28 $; the paid tier (20 $ per user per month) breaks even at 0.714 h = 43 min saved per user per month; the setup pays back in 1.23 monthsBrick 3 and Class 3 formulas
RQ3 (Research Question 3)the pilot group (S1–S3) went from 35.85 to 13.73 min per run (−22.12); the comparison group (S4–S5) from 34.67 to 34.10 (−0.57)14 days, n = 27 → 15 runs and 18 → 10 runs

The comparison group matters. Its change (−0.57 min) estimates what would have happened to everyone without the assistant (a quieter week, practice). The difference of the changes, (−22.12) − (−0.57) = −21.55 min per run, is the estimated effect of the assistant; economists call this design difference-in-differences (DiD) (MRU (Marginal Revolution University) course pageVirusTotal).

The expected impact follows in three lines: 21.55 − 2.00 min of human review = 19.55 min saved per run; × 100 runs per month = 1 955 min = 32.6 hours per month; × 28 $/h = ≈ 912 $ per month.

▣ Slide 41 · The recommendation: six parts

10.4The recommendation: finding, evidence, decision, impact, risk

In Class 7 you wrote recommendations in four parts. For the report, add the impact and the alternatives considered:

RuleFinding. Assistant-triaged e-mail took 21.55 minutes less per run than the change observed in the comparison group. Evidence. 14 working days of timed runs; pilot S1–S3 (27 runs before, 15 after) against comparison S4–S5 (18 before, 10 after). Decision. Automate e-mail triage first, for all five staff members, on the free tier with the offline fallback. Impact. About 32.6 hours and 912 $ per month after a 2-minute human review of each run. Risk. 14 days and five people; a possible novelty effect in the first week; the daily quota of the free tier (the fallback keeps the brief running); no message text is stored. Alternatives. The paid tier is justified only if it saves more than 43 minutes per user per month beyond the free tier; doing nothing keeps about 1 640 $ per month of manual triage.

Each sentence of the recommendation must point to a result in the report. A decision without a number is an opinion; a number without a decision is not yet a recommendation.

▣ Slides 42–43 · The technical report: structure

10.4The technical report: structure and the Brick → section map

The Final grades a technical report of at least 8 pages including figures (Appendix B). Its sections, in order: Title · Abstract · 1 Introduction and Problem · 2 Requirements · 3 Method · 4 Design · 5 Implementation · 6 Testing · 7 Results · 8 Discussion and Recommendation · 9 Conclusion · References · Appendices (testing log, code-review evidence, Actions run history, data sheets).

The abstract summarises the whole report in at most 150 words: the problem, the method, the key result and the recommendation. Write it last, when the results are final. Tables and figures are numbered and captioned; references follow APA (American Psychological Association) 7.

Nothing is written from zero: each Brick already holds a section.

10.4Academic honesty, the rubric and the three sprints

Cite everything you used: textbooks and articles, documentation pages, code you reused (with its address and licence), datasets, and generative AI (Artificial Intelligence). Since September 2025 the APA (American Psychological Association) Style team recommends referencing a specific AI chat: Company. (Year, Month Day). Title of the chat [Generative AI chat]. Tool or model. URL (Uniform Resource Locator) of the chat (APA Part 1VirusTotal). When AI was used only to find sources, cite the sources it found, not the AI (APA Part 2VirusTotal). Describe in §3 Method how and where AI assistance was used (Legal Notice §18 Academic integrity).

What the Final grades. Five rubric dimensions: Methodology · Tech Implementation · Analytical Rigor · Lab Proficiency · Communication. Suggested split of the 40 %: report 15 · working assistant and codebase 15 · demonstration and presentation 10 (confirmed in class before January 15).

▣ Slide 46 · Real-life example 10.4 and Code 10.4
Real-life example 10.4 — From the pilot numbers to the owner's decision
Task of the exampleCompute the answers to RQ1 (Research Question 1)–RQ3 (Research Question 3) from boreal_routines_2026.csv, draw the four charts, write the recommendation with impact and risk, and generate the skeleton of the technical report with numbered figures.How it relates to the lectureIt applies the distinction between result and conclusion, the choice of chart per question, the recommendation pattern with impact, and the report structure.

The owner's message (Friday, 17:40). "I have ten minutes on Monday morning. Tell me what to automate first, what it saves per month, and what could go wrong. One page."

What the team does. The program results_to_report.py reads the 420 runs and computes, for each routine, the mean minutes and the monthly cost; it ranks the routines (RQ1 (Research Question 1)). It computes the coefficient of variation of each routine. It compares the e-mail pilot with the comparison group and derives the difference of the changes, the net saving per run, the hours and the dollars per month (RQ3 (Research Question 3)). It prints a results table and the recommendation in the five-part pattern, then writes the headings of docs/report.md with the figure list.

The page the owner reads. Three sentences from the recommendation, Figure 1 (monthly cost per routine) and Figure 4 (before/after bars). Everything else is in the report for the Final.

Code 10.4 — run it step by step

Task of the program. The program reads boreal_routines_2026.csv and computes the monthly cost of every routine (RQ1 (Research Question 1)), the coefficient of variation of the manual runs (RQ1), the break-even of the paid tier (RQ2 (Research Question 2)) and the pilot effect with the comparison group (RQ3 (Research Question 3)). It then derives the impact in hours and dollars, prints the recommendation in five parts and the headings of docs/report.md.
How it relates to the lecture. It illustrates Real-life example 10.4: every printed sentence is a result with its evidence, the recommendation is built only from those results, and the skeleton is the report structure of the Final.
Run it yourself. python results_to_report.py (data/boreal_routines_2026.csv next to the script or one folder up)
Code 10.4 — results_to_report.py: from 420 runs to RQ1 (Research Question 1)–RQ3 (Research Question 3), the recommendation and the report skeleton
Visualization · Charts and numbers as the program computes them
Variables of the current frame
Console · what the program printed
Execution steps · click any step to inspect it
The player replays a real run of the file, recorded line by line; long loops are shortened. Pause at any moment and click a step to see its line, variables and output.

Step-by-step explanation of Code 10.4

  1. Constants. 28 $/h, 100 runs per month, 20 $ for the paid tier, 2 minutes of review, the pilot group S1–S3 and the pilot start date: every assumption is named once at the top, so the report can cite it.
  2. find_data and load. pathlib builds the path from the script's own folder; csv.DictReader returns 420 dictionaries. The player collapses repeated loop lines after four passes, so you see the pattern without 420 identical steps.
  3. RQ1 (Research Question 1) — monthly bill. defaultdict(list) groups the minutes of the manual and template runs per routine; each mean × 100 × 28 / 60 gives a monthly cost; the dictionary is sorted from the most expensive routine. The panel draws the sorted bar chart as the values arrive.
  4. RQ1 (Research Question 1) — variability. cv_manual divides the sample SD (Standard Deviation) by the mean for each routine; max(cv, key=cv.get) returns standup_notes (26.4 %).
  5. RQ2 (Research Question 2) — break-even. 20 / 28 = 0.714 h = 43 minutes per user per month.
  6. RQ3 (Research Question 3) — difference of the changes. pilot_effect splits the e-mail runs into four groups (pilot/comparison × before/after) by staff member and date. Pilot 35.85 → 13.73 (−22.12), comparison 34.67 → 34.10 (−0.57); the difference is −21.55 min per run. The panel shows the before/after bars of both groups.
  7. Impact. 21.55 − 2 = 19.55 min per run; × 100 runs = 1 955 min = 32.6 h; × 28 $ = 912 $ per month.
  8. Recommendation and skeleton. The five sentences (finding, evidence, decision, impact, risk) reuse the computed variables, so the text can never disagree with the numbers. The last line lists the thirteen headings of docs/report.md.

Figure 10.4

Key terms

result — A number or table with its evidence (data, method, n) and its limits.
discussion — Interpretation of the results for the reader: meaning, comparison with expectations, limits.
conclusion — The answer to one research question, using only results already presented.
comparison group — Staff without the change (S4–S5), whose change estimates what would have happened anyway.
difference of the changes — Change of the pilot group minus change of the comparison group: −21.55 min per run (difference-in-differences).
expected impact — The saving in hours and dollars per month implied by a result: 32.6 h and ≈ 912 $.
recommendation — Finding, evidence, decision, impact, risk and alternatives, each tied to a result.
abstract — At most 150 words: problem, method, key result, recommendation; written last.
figure caption — "Figure n." with a short italic title; every figure is cited in the text.
Project Sprint — Supervised work session with a brief, a Q&A (Questions and Answers) board and a checkpoint (Dec 4, 11, 18).

The five workshop steps

Each step is shown as a short GIF (Graphics Interchange Format) animation of the terminal or the editor; use the button under a step to save its animation.

Step 1 · Install and pin pytest

Inside the activated virtual environment: python -m pip install pytest, then add the exact version to requirements.txt (pytest==… as printed by pip freeze) next to matplotlib.

✓ Check: requirements.txt lists pytest with ==, and python -m pytest --version prints the same version on every member's machine.

Step 2 · Write six tests and turn them green

tests/test_stats_engine.py (3 tests) and tests/test_econ_engine.py (3 tests): one edge case (empty list or zero hourly value) and one oracle test (statistics.stdev). Run python -m pytest -q until the last line says 6 passed (or more).

✓ Check: The run ends with N passed and no F or E; the exit code is 0.

Step 3 · Add ci.yml and watch Actions

Copy ci.yml from Appendix D.3 into .github/workflows/, commit and push. Open the Actions tab: the run must end with a green check.

✓ Check: The commit on GitHub shows a green check produced by the ci workflow.

Step 4 · Create the report skeleton

docs/report.md with Title, Abstract and sections 1–9, References and Appendices; two sentences under each heading; paste the Brick → section map at the end.

✓ Check: Every heading of the Final's report structure is present, each with two sentences.

docs/buglog.md with three real issues from docs/issues.md. Then git add -A, git commit -m "Brick 9: tests + report skeleton", git tag -a beta-0.1 -m "Brick 9", git push, git push origin --tags.
